title: How the Globe of Death Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the Globe of Death, the steel-mesh sphere motorcycle stunt seen at circuses and fairs. They cover its origins (bicycle and unicycle versions in the 1900s, Arthur Rosenthal's 1904 patent from Grand Rapids, Michigan), its spread to Europe and South America, and performers like Jose Urias and Babs (first loop-to-loop, reportedly 1,003 loops). They discuss modern split and triple-split globes, bike modifications emphasizing torque over horsepower, and the physics of centripetal force, normal force, gravity, and G-forces, including comparisons to Colonel John Paul Stapp and Guy Martin's wall of death record. The episode also includes a Tesla torque anecdote, a sketch show and live event promo, and a listener email about whether a Spanish flu-style epidemic could happen again.

segments.title: Live show promo and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck promote San Francisco Sketch Fest and a Movie Crush Live event, then banter about the phrase 'Globe of Death' and its Spanish translations.

segments.title: What the Globe of Death is
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Globe of Death as a steel mesh sphere where one or more motorcycle riders loop around inside, with record numbers of riders (seven seen on video) and its circus origins as a marketing name.

segments.title: Origins: bicycles, Arthur Rosenthal and the 1904 patent
segments.summary: Early globe acts used bicycles and unicycles in Europe in the 1900s. Arthur Rosenthal, with partner Frank Lemon, received a patent on May 3, 1904, in Grand Rapids, Michigan. Motorcycles later became the standard vehicle, and the act spread to South America, where Jose Urias performed by about 1912.

segments.title: Performers, records and golden age
segments.summary: Performers Speedy Wilson, Speedy McNish, and Babs are mentioned; Babs is credited as the first to do a loop-to-loop and reportedly logged 1,003 loops, a record that has not been broken. The hosts note a golden age between the world wars and later corporate circus acceptance in the early 2000s.

segments.title: Size, danger and split and triple-split globes
segments.summary: Globes are typically about sixteen feet in diameter. Early acts were very dangerous. Split globes, where the top lifts away, were popularized by the Urias family, and the Torres family introduced a triple split globe with a narrow middle band.

segments.title: Bikes, G-forces and torque
segments.summary: Riders use modified lightweight dirt bikes. Speeds are around 40 to 60 mph with 3.5 to 4.5 Gs. Torque matters more than horsepower. The hosts tell a Tesla anecdote about rapid acceleration and torque, and mention an aerialist wife performing inside the globe.

segments.title: Physics of the Globe of Death
segments.summary: The hosts explain centripetal force, normal force, and gravity. Centripetal force comes from the globe wall pushing riders inward. G-forces are the apparent increase in weight from circular motion, and too many Gs can cause blackout. They compare to a key on a string, a steel drum carnival ride, and James Bond G-force scenes. Colonel John Paul Stapp and Guy Martin's wall of death record are mentioned.

segments.title: Listener mail: could a Spanish flu-style epidemic happen again
segments.summary: Jasmine, a Master's of Public Health candidate, writes that another flu epidemic could happen, citing crowded meat industry conditions, viral mutation, CDC budget cuts, and low public concern about influenza.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts give social media and email contact information and sign off.
